title: Adolescent Health: Private Time, Capacity, Confidentiality, and Safety
bottomLine: Adolescent care requires routine private time, developmentally appropriate consent/capacity assessment and clear explanation of confidentiality and its limits. Privacy improves disclosure and access to care; safety threats, maltreatment and legal reporting duties can override confidentiality according to applicable Canadian law.
recognize: Adolescents may withhold sexual health, substance use, mood, violence or identity concerns if private care is not offered.
Decision-making capacity is based on understanding/appreciation and applicable provincial law, not a universal Canada-wide age.
differentiate: Confidentiality is not secrecy without limits; imminent serious safety risk, child-protection duties and some reportable conditions can require disclosure.
Parental involvement can be highly supportive but should not automatically replace the capable adolescent's voice.
assessment: Provide private time and assess mood/suicide, relationships/violence, sexual/reproductive health, substance use, school, sleep, safety, identity and chronic-disease self-management using nonjudgmental language.
workup: Testing is risk/symptom driven; do not order STI, pregnancy, toxicology or mental-health testing simply because the patient is an adolescent without a clinical indication.
management: Offer confidential prevention/treatment within scope and law, involve caregivers with the adolescent's consent when appropriate, and escalate immediate safety concerns.
Use closed-loop transition planning for chronic illness as adolescents move toward adult care.
medicationSafety: Review privacy implications of prescriptions, pharmacy notifications, portals/billing and caregiver access when these could unintentionally disclose sensitive care.
counselling: Explain confidentiality before sensitive questions, including exactly when information may need to be shared for safety or legal reasons.
followUp: Arrange accessible confidential follow-up and confirm referrals/tests can be accessed without unintended disclosure where possible.
examTrap: Refusing confidential sexual or mental-health care solely because a parent is present—or promising absolute secrecy despite a serious safety threat.
oneLinePearl: Adolescent confidentiality is a clinical intervention with clear safety and legal limits.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society — Privacy and confidentiality in adolescent health care
CPS comprehensive sexual health assessment guidance

title: Pediatric Mental Health Screening: Screening Opens the Assessment, It Does Not Finish It
bottomLine: Mental-health screening identifies possible problems; diagnosis and safety planning require interview, function, developmental context, family/school information and direct suicide/self-harm assessment when indicated. A low score does not overrule a concerning history or observed deterioration.
recognize: Anxiety, depression, ADHD, trauma, eating disorders, substance use and somatic symptoms can present through school decline, irritability, sleep change, pain or family conflict rather than a named psychiatric complaint.
differentiate: Normal developmental distress differs from persistent impairment, safety risk or loss of function.
Medical disease, medication/substance effects and neurodevelopmental conditions can mimic psychiatric symptoms.
assessment: Assess symptoms, duration, function, school/family context, bullying/violence, sleep, substances, eating, psychosis/mania and suicide/self-harm risk; obtain private adolescent interview when appropriate.
workup: Use validated age-appropriate tools as adjuncts and order medical testing only when a plausible mimic/contributor exists.
management: Use stepped, evidence-based psychosocial and pharmacologic care matched to diagnosis/severity and access.
Active suicidality, psychosis, severe eating-disorder instability, mania or inability to maintain safety requires urgent in-person psychiatric/medical assessment.
medicationSafety: Psychotropic medication requires indication-, age- and drug-specific monitoring; screen for bipolarity/activation risk before reflex antidepressant escalation and monitor metabolic/movement effects when antipsychotics are used.
redFlags: Severe aggression or inability to maintain safety
counselling: Normalize asking about mental health and explain that questionnaires help start the conversation rather than label the child.
followUp: Track function and safety after treatment changes and close the loop on psychotherapy/specialty referrals.
examTrap: Using a negative screening questionnaire as the main reason to ignore active self-harm or severe functional decline.
oneLinePearl: Screening is a doorway; clinical assessment determines diagnosis and safety.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society child and youth mental-health resources
CPS mental-health screening tools and rating scales

title: Child Maltreatment: Stabilize, Document Objectively, Report Suspicion, Avoid Repeated Interrogation
bottomLine: The clinician does not need proof of maltreatment before acting on a reasonable concern. Treat urgent injuries, use a trauma-informed medical assessment, document observations and spontaneous statements objectively, avoid repeated leading questioning, and make the legally required report to the appropriate child-welfare authority according to jurisdiction.
recognize: Concern rises with injury inconsistent with developmental ability/history, patterned injury, concerning bruising location, sentinel injuries in nonmobile infants, delay in care or repeated unexplained injuries.
A normal physical examination does not exclude sexual abuse.
differentiate: Medical mimics such as bleeding/bone/skin disorders must be considered without using them to delay protection when maltreatment concern is reasonable.
Forensic interviewing is a specialized process; the medical history should gather enough information for care/safety without repeatedly interrogating the child.
assessment: Stabilize first, obtain medical/developmental history, document exact caregiver/child statements where relevant, complete careful head-to-toe examination and assess immediate safety/siblings/other vulnerable children.
workup: Use age/injury-specific skeletal survey, neuroimaging, bleeding-disorder, STI/pregnancy/forensic evidence or other testing through current child-maltreatment protocols and expertise.
management: Treat injuries and urgent medical needs, involve child-maltreatment specialists when available and report concerns directly to child protective services as required by applicable law.
Coordinate a safe disposition; do not discharge to an unsafe environment merely because testing is incomplete.
medicationSafety: Provide STI/HIV/pregnancy prophylaxis/treatment or analgesia when clinically indicated without allowing evidence collection to delay necessary care.
redFlags: Child in medical danger from neglect
counselling: Use non-blaming language, thank the child for telling when disclosure occurs and avoid promising outcomes you cannot guarantee.
followUp: Ensure child-welfare, medical, mental-health and specialty follow-up are closed-loop and document who owns each action.
examTrap: Waiting for definitive proof before reporting a reasonable child-protection concern—or repeatedly questioning a child to make the history 'more certain'.
oneLinePearl: Recognize, stabilize, document, report and protect; investigation belongs to the appropriate specialist systems.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society Child and Youth Maltreatment resources
CPS pre-pubertal sexual abuse statement reaffirmed 2026
CPS traumatic head injury due to child maltreatment guidance

title: Pediatric Toxicology: Substance, Dose, Time, Formulation, and Symptoms
bottomLine: Pediatric poisoning management starts with ABCs and a precise exposure history: substance, formulation/concentration, maximum possible dose, time, route, co-ingestants, symptoms and child weight. Contact the regional poison centre early; do not induce vomiting or apply a universal decontamination rule.
recognize: High-risk exposures include opioids, acetaminophen, iron, salicylates, calcium-channel/beta blockers, sulfonylureas, clonidine, caustics, hydrocarbons, button batteries and multiple magnets.
Small amounts can be dangerous in a small child and modified-release products can delay toxicity.
differentiate: An asymptomatic child after a low-risk taste differs from a potentially lethal single-pill exposure.
Button-battery/magnet/caustic ingestions follow urgent procedural pathways and should not be managed like routine medication overdose.
assessment: Assess airway/breathing/circulation, mental status, glucose, vital signs, toxidrome, access to medications/chemicals, intentionality in adolescents and exact product information.
workup: Use poison-centre guided ECG, glucose, acetaminophen/salicylate levels, electrolytes/acid-base, imaging or drug-specific testing when clinically indicated.
management: Stabilize first, use substance-specific antidote/supportive care and consult the poison centre/toxicology.
Do not induce emesis; activated charcoal, whole-bowel irrigation, enhanced elimination and antidotes are exposure-specific decisions.
medicationSafety: Do not rely on a remembered universal antidote dose/protocol when contemporary poison-centre guidance is available.
Acetaminophen/N-acetylcysteine protocols can be updated; follow the current Canadian poison-centre pathway.
counselling: After stabilization, address safe storage and adolescent mental-health/suicide risk when ingestion was intentional.
followUp: Ensure delayed-toxicity observation/follow-up meets the poison-centre recommendation and close mental-health/safeguarding actions.
examTrap: Giving activated charcoal or inducing vomiting automatically before identifying the substance, timing, airway status and contraindications.
oneLinePearl: Poisoning care is exposure-specific; poison-centre guidance beats a memorized universal recipe.

title: Pediatric Allergy: Anaphylaxis First, Sensitization Is Not Clinical Allergy
bottomLine: Allergy diagnosis requires a compatible clinical history; a positive skin or specific-IgE test alone shows sensitization, not necessarily clinical allergy. Suspected anaphylaxis is a clinical emergency treated promptly with intramuscular epinephrine rather than antihistamine-first care.
recognize: IgE-mediated reactions usually occur rapidly after exposure and can involve skin/mucosa, respiratory compromise, hypotension or persistent GI symptoms.
Atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, food allergy, drug allergy and venom allergy have different diagnostic pathways.
differentiate: Food intolerance and viral rash differ from immediate reproducible allergy; broad panel testing can generate clinically irrelevant sensitization.
Large local insect-sting reactions differ from systemic anaphylaxis.
assessment: Document exact exposure, dose/route, timing, reproducibility, organ systems involved, treatment response, asthma control, cofactors and family access to emergency medication.
workup: Use targeted allergy testing/referral based on history; oral challenge is specialist/safety-context dependent and contraindicated when severe reaction history makes unsupervised challenge unsafe.
management: Treat anaphylaxis immediately with IM epinephrine and emergency supportive care.
Provide allergen-specific avoidance without unnecessary dietary restriction and refer systemic venom/drug/food cases when diagnostic clarification or immunotherapy is indicated.
medicationSafety: Antihistamines do not replace epinephrine for airway/breathing/circulatory anaphylaxis.
Review auto-injector dose/device as the child grows and optimize asthma because poorly controlled asthma increases reaction risk.
redFlags: Food allergy plus poorly controlled asthma
counselling: Teach written emergency plan, epinephrine technique and school/daycare preparedness while avoiding fear-based overrestriction.
followUp: Reassess diagnosis, growth/nutrition and device dose/technique; allergist follow-up is appropriate for significant systemic allergy.
examTrap: Diagnosing multiple food allergies from a broad positive IgE panel without a compatible clinical reaction—or treating anaphylaxis with antihistamine first.
oneLinePearl: Clinical reaction defines allergy; epinephrine defines first-line anaphylaxis treatment.

title: Pediatric Endocrine Disorders: Growth, Puberty, Glucose, and Adrenal/Thyroid Emergencies
bottomLine: Pediatric endocrine disease is recognized through trajectories—growth, puberty, weight and glucose—plus age-specific emergencies. DKA, adrenal crisis, severe hypoglycemia and symptomatic electrolyte disorders require immediate stabilization; chronic short stature or pubertal variation needs pattern-based evaluation rather than one laboratory panel.
recognize: Type 1 diabetes can present with polyuria/polydipsia/weight loss or DKA; thyroid disease affects growth/puberty/energy; adrenal disease can cause hypotension/electrolyte disturbance.
Endocrine causes of short stature often reduce height velocity and may preserve/increase weight, unlike many systemic/nutritional causes.
differentiate: Familial short stature/constitutional delay differ from endocrine/systemic disease by trajectory, bone-age/puberty/family pattern.
DKA is ketone/acidosis physiology, not glucose level alone; SGLT2 exposure is uncommon in children but illness/insulin omission remain key triggers.
assessment: Plot accurate growth/BMI, review puberty stage, family heights/puberty, symptoms, medications including steroids, glucose symptoms, BP, hydration and skin/thyroid findings.
workup: Use targeted glucose/A1C/ketones/electrolytes, TSH/free T4, celiac/IGF/bone-age or adrenal testing according to the phenotype and specialist pathway.
management: Stabilize DKA/hypoglycemia/adrenal crisis through pediatric protocols and involve endocrine expertise.
For chronic growth/puberty disease, treat the cause and refer when trajectory or endocrine findings are abnormal.
medicationSafety: Insulin is high-alert and weight/meal/activity sensitive; type 1 diabetes requires basal insulin continuity with illness/NPO adjustment rather than complete omission.
Chronic glucocorticoids can suppress growth/HPA axis and must not be stopped abruptly when adrenal suppression is plausible.
redFlags: Rapid growth/puberty regression or CNS symptoms
counselling: Teach sick-day/ketone/hypoglycemia plans and frame growth/puberty variation without stigma.
followUp: Trend growth, puberty and disease-specific labs with pediatric endocrinology when indicated.
examTrap: Ordering a broad endocrine panel for a child tracking normally at a low familial percentile—or holding all insulin in type 1 diabetes because the child is not eating.
oneLinePearl: Pediatric endocrine diagnosis lives in the trajectory; endocrine emergencies live in physiology.

title: Pediatric Neurology: Development, Localization, Seizure Safety, and Raised ICP
bottomLine: Pediatric neurologic assessment starts with development, baseline function, localization and tempo. Ongoing seizure/status, meningitis/encephalitis, acute focal deficit, raised intracranial pressure, shunt failure and progressive weakness/bulbar-respiratory symptoms require urgent pathways; routine headache or a single simple febrile seizure is different.
recognize: Seizures, headache, weakness, developmental regression, altered gait, abnormal tone and school/cognitive change can represent neurologic disease.
Hydrocephalus/shunt problems in younger children may present with vomiting, irritability, lethargy or head-growth changes rather than a classic adult headache.
differentiate: Syncope can include brief jerks but generally has rapid recovery; migraine can cause focal aura but a first acute focal deficit needs stroke/structural evaluation.
Simple febrile seizure differs from prolonged/focal/recurrent-within-illness events that need broader assessment.
assessment: Assess ABCs/glucose first when altered/seizing, then onset/tempo, fever, trauma, developmental baseline, focal findings, head circumference when age appropriate, shunt history, medications/substances and family history.
workup: Use EEG, MRI/CT, CSF, metabolic/infectious studies only according to the syndrome; do not routinely neuroimage every uncomplicated primary headache or simple febrile seizure.
management: Treat ongoing convulsive seizure through current pediatric emergency protocol and escalate status epilepticus.

Urgently evaluate CNS infection, raised ICP/shunt failure, acute focal deficit or progressive neuromuscular respiratory weakness; stable chronic disorders require neurology/developmental coordination.
medicationSafety: Antiseizure drugs have agent-specific monitoring and interaction/reproductive implications; do not abruptly discontinue chronic therapy without an emergency/specialist plan.
Sedating drugs can mask neurologic deterioration.
counselling: Teach seizure first aid, water/heights safety and individualized school/action plans where relevant.
followUp: Close EEG/imaging/specialty referrals and track development/function, not just event count.
examTrap: Ordering CT for every recurrent migraine while missing progressive morning vomiting and papilledema—or treating prolonged seizure as routine febrile seizure.
oneLinePearl: Pediatric neurology is development plus localization plus tempo; emergencies declare themselves through physiology and function.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society pediatric seizure/emergency resources
Choosing Wisely Canada pediatric neurology diagnostic stewardship

title: Pediatric Urgent Care Triage: Appearance, ABCs, Perfusion, Hydration, and Trajectory
bottomLine: Pediatric triage is not adult triage with smaller vital signs. Age-adjust physiology, appearance/interaction, work of breathing, perfusion and hydration determine urgency. A child can compensate until sudden decompensation, so worsening tachycardia, mental status or work of breathing matters before hypotension appears.
recognize: Abnormal appearance, increased work of breathing and poor circulation/perfusion are high-yield global danger signals.
Infants and medically complex children may deteriorate with subtle feeding, tone or interaction changes.
differentiate: Fever height or pain score alone does not define severity; a calm lethargic infant can be sicker than a crying febrile toddler.
Normal BP does not exclude compensated shock in children.
assessment: Use pediatric ABCDE assessment, age-appropriate vitals, weight, glucose when indicated, interaction/mental status, respiratory effort, perfusion/cap refill, hydration/urine output and caregiver concern/trajectory.
workup: Testing follows the stabilization/differential; do not delay airway, oxygenation, glucose, seizure or shock treatment for diagnostic completeness.
management: Escalate airway compromise, respiratory failure, shock, altered consciousness, severe dehydration, sepsis, anaphylaxis, toxic ingestion and surgical emergencies immediately.
For discharge, require improving physiology, oral/hydration feasibility, caregiver understanding and reliable return/follow-up plan.
medicationSafety: Weight in kilograms and concentration verification are mandatory for high-risk pediatric medication dosing; avoid pounds-to-kilograms and decimal errors.
Sedation/analgesia should be appropriate and monitored rather than withheld because the patient is a child.
counselling: Give specific symptom-based return precautions and verify caregiver understanding rather than saying only 'come back if worse'.
followUp: Close pending results/referrals and ensure high-risk infants/complex children have an appropriate reassessment interval.
examTrap: Waiting for hypotension before recognizing pediatric shock or using adult-normal vital ranges for an infant.
oneLinePearl: In children, appearance, breathing and perfusion deteriorate before blood pressure tells you the whole story.
